item.title: History-making Miss USA reveals how she got swimsuit-ready while raising 2 young kids
item.description: Justus Kelley reveals how she prepped for the Miss USA pageant during nap times and bath routines while caring for her two young foster children.
item.content:encoded:
Justus Kelley made history as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss USA — and she got there in an unconventional way.

On Aug. 27, the organization hosted the 75th edition of the national pageant in Miami. The 31-year-old, who was Miss Virginia USA 2026, succeeded last year’s winner, Audrey Eckert, 24. The pageant opened the competition to married women and mothers in 2023.

"My pageant prep, it did look different," Kelley told Fox News Digital. "I'm not going to pretend like I was able to dedicate the same amount of time as what I did in the past. I had to get creative. Their nap time was my prep time. It was late nights. It was after the bath and bed routine. I did walking classes with my baby on my chest, in his carrier. I did squats in my living room while holding my two-year-old. I practiced interview questions while feeding my toddler."

NAVY VETERAN TRADES MILITARY UNIFORM FOR MISS GEORGIA SASH FOLLOWING HEARTBREAKING LOSS

"There were days when I wished I could just take the entire day to dedicate to pageant prep, but that's not where I am," Kelley said. "That's not the season of life that I'm in. And we made it work, and my family was fully on board with this experience. They know that they're along for the journey; they're along for this ride with me."

The Miss USA pageant began in 1952 in Long Beach, California, with New York's Jackie Loughery becoming its first winner. The competition is separate from the Miss America pageant, which traces its history to a 1921 event in Atlantic City, New Jersey.

Kelley, a foster mom of two, is the first married mother to retain the Miss USA title. In 1957, Mary Leona Gage was crowned Miss USA but was stripped of the title the following day after pageant organizers learned she was married and the mother of two sons.

WATCH: MISS USA 2026 REVEALS HOW SHE TRAINED FOR PAGEANT WITH KIDS IN TOW

Kelley said she ditched social media and TV in favor of workouts whenever she found a spare moment while caring for her two young children.

"I love abductor and adductor exercises, something that I usually do on a machine at the gym," she explained. "But if I can't make it to the gym, I'm just lying on the floor, elevating my leg and mirroring what I would've done on that machine. For me, leading up to a pageant, knowing there's a fitness component, I'm going to be in a swimsuit on that stage. I want to feel good. I want to show off all this hard work."

"I really focused on core," she said. "So a lot of times you'll find me at home in the living room. I might be watching a movie or doing some self-care, but I am on the floor crunching it out during that movie, saying, 'Let's try to get through this whole scene doing crunches,' and then you pause. It was really all about focusing on core."

Kelley said her husband's support also helped her through the competition.

"The crown might be his because all he keeps saying is, 'I can't believe I'm Mr. USA,'" Kelley said with a laugh, referring to her college sweetheart. "I'm like, 'Babe, I don't know if that might be trademarked. Stop saying that!'"

"He is so over the moon," Kelley said. "We've been together for 13, going on 14 years and married for nine. He's been a part of every bit of this journey. I've been competing for over 10 years now. And from my very first pageant, he was there holding a sign with my face on it up until the very end. I did not get here alone. He's been a huge supporter. My husband's a consultant, and he's been calling himself my pageant consultant. But he's been a huge help in getting me to this point."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

This year's prize package, valued at more than $685,000, includes a $150,000 salary, a Range Rover, a one-year lease at a luxury Miami apartment, a Westgate Vacation Home Club membership and a $30,000 Miss Universe wardrobe, according to People magazine.

"The prize that made me go, 'Wow, and I have some questions,' was knowing that the Range Rover is a part of traveling in style even after your year as Miss USA. I think that's huge. But my first question was, 'Does it fit car seats?'"

Kelley said she wants her year as Miss USA to challenge the idea that women need to choose between their families, careers and personal dreams.

"You don't have to choose one part of who you are," Kelley said. "You can be all of who you are. That, to me, is the message. We can embrace every part of who we are. It doesn't take away from the other. It doesn't mean there aren't trade-offs, and there aren't times when we have to lean on our village more heavily to get through all the things that we may be pursuing. But know that we don't have to sacrifice ourselves."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Looking ahead, Kelley said her victory wasn't only personal — she also saw it as a chance to represent mothers and wives balancing family life with their own ambitions.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Knowing that history was made as the first mom, as the first wife, as the first woman in her 30s, my first thought was how amazing it is to get to do this and to represent women from all over the country, from all over the world that resonate with, 'Hey, we're still dreaming,'" she said.

"We're raising our families, but we still have dreams. We still have things that we want to go after and pursue. But what an honor. I get to do this. I get to represent these women. What an honor."

item.title: Costco brings back a fan-favorite food court treat after years off the menu
item.description: Costco's twisted churro is back in U.S. food courts for a limited time at $1.49, but fans are already demanding it stay permanently on the menu.
item.content:encoded:
Costco fans who have spent the last two years begging for one discontinued food court favorite to be brought back are finally getting their wish.

The retailer announced Friday that its twisted churros will return to U.S. food courts for a limited time, ending speculation after the company teased the comeback on social media.

Earlier in the week, Costco teased the announcement with a cryptic Instagram video showing two employees discussing a mystery menu item before its name was bleeped out, prompting fans to flood the comments with guesses ranging from the meat-and-vegetable-topped combo pizza to the Polish hot dog and acai bowl.

COSTCO SHOPPERS CHALLENGE INFLUENCER'S CLAIM THAT 'INSANE' CHICKEN MEAL CAN FEED FAMILY OF FIVE

Many correctly guessed the cinnamon-sugar dessert, which was pulled from menus in 2024, according to reports and social media users.

"The Churro is BACK in U.S. food courts for a limited time!" the warehouse club announced Friday. "Look out for it at your local warehouse over the coming weeks as exact launch dates vary."

MCDONALD'S NEWEST MENU ITEM HAS FANS BEGGING FOR ONE DISCONTINUED FAVORITE

The treat is expected to cost $1.49, the same price as before it was discontinued, according to reports.

Many social media users rejoiced.

"Dreams do come true," one man commented on Instagram. "FINALLY," another one wrote.

COSTCO FANS ERUPT AFTER BELOVED FOOD COURT ITEM REPLACED BY HIGH-CALORIE NEWCOMER

"The scream my kid just screamed," a mom commented.

But not everyone was satisfied.

"LIMITED TIME???? NO. YOU KEEP IT ON THERE!" one Instagram user exclaimed.

"Limited time better be the next 50 years," said another.

Other people were disappointed that the twisted churro, which was reportedly introduced in 2021, was being brought back and not the classic straight version that dates back to the 1990s — which only cost 99 cents.

"We meant the old school straight churros, not these twisted imposters," one person said.

Others were still hung up on the pizza of the past.

"Combo pizza next please!" one said.

The announcement marks the latest change to Costco's closely watched, low-priced food court menu, which has developed a dedicated fan base.

This year alone, Costco added chicken tenders nationwide and a hot dog-and-water-bottle combo while continuing to test other menu items.

Costco tried to satisfy fans earlier this year by adding mini churro bites to a $2.99 caramel sundae, but many shoppers said it wasn't the same as the full-size food court churro they had been requesting, Fox News Digital previously reported.

It's unclear how long the churro will be on menus for.

item.title: Tropical disease spread by mosquitoes claims first recorded death in southern US state
item.description: Gay Small died on her 80th birthday from dengue after a mosquito bite near her Tampa home, the Florida Department of Health confirmed Friday.
item.content:encoded:
Florida recorded its first confirmed dengue fever death of 2026 earlier this month, according to the Florida Department of Health.

Gay Small of Hillsborough County died on Sept. 4 — her 80th birthday — from complications of a dengue infection, including septic shock and multi-organ failure, after she was bitten by a mosquito near her home on Bayshore Boulevard, the Tampa Bay Times reported.

"Cheated, just, you know, it’s so unfair because she was in good health, and she worked hard to stay healthy, and she walked, and she ate right and you know, all the things that you’re supposed to do," Small's daughter, Anna Small, told Tampa's WFLA Channel 8.

DANGEROUS MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS SPREADS IN ONE STATE AS OFFICIALS WARN OF RISING CASES

"And you know, this virus just kind of comes out of nowhere. She met the wrong mosquito, and that’s it," Anna Small said.

Small's family said they believe Gay Small first caught dengue years ago while traveling abroad but didn't know it. People who have had dengue before are much more likely to develop severe symptoms.

"While in the hospital, Small said her mother was weak, her hands turned red, and she had trembles that she could hear in her voice," reported WFLA. "She had to go into the ICU by the middle of the week."

Small's late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working on dengue vaccines, according to the couple's daughter.

The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death Friday after completing its investigation, but did not release additional information, WFLA reported.

The Times, citing University of South Florida public-health instructor Kristi Miley, reported that a dengue death had not been recorded in the Tampa Bay area in nearly a century.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

Florida mosquito-control agencies have stepped up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as locally acquired dengue fever cases — which means people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad — have climbed in recent weeks.

The Times reported that since July, Florida "has been experiencing an unprecedented outbreak of locally caught cases." Hillsborough County, where Small lived, "has been at the epicenter of the epidemic."

Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.

"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day," he said.

"When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."

In addition to increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services has also been inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.

The increased application of insecticide and larvicide by helicopters appears to be working, the Times reported, as, "Of the last 1,500 mosquitoes they've sent for testing, all have returned negative for dengue."

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.

The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic. In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

item.title: 'Shut up' and listen: Trace Gallagher shares 'unexpected' wisdom learned from being a 'girl dad'
item.description: Fox News' Trace Gallagher shares with Fox News Digital the parenting lesson that transformed his bond with his daughters, from a youth soccer moment to learning when to stay silent.
item.content:encoded:
For 30 years as a broadcast news anchor, Fox News chief breaking news correspondent Trace Gallagher has built his career on knowing exactly what to say when the camera turns on.

Yet when it comes to raising daughters in an increasingly hyper-connected and chaotic world, the veteran newsman says the most powerful tool in a father’s arsenal is paying attention in silence. 

"These are different people," Gallagher said with a smile about his two daughters, now 25 and 22. "When they have a problem, they don’t really want you to talk to them about their problem. They just want you to hear them about the problem. You need to sit, you need to shut up and you need to listen."

TRACE GALLAGHER: COMMON SENSE IS ALIVE IN AMERICA, WE JUST NEED TO LISTEN 

In an era defined by fast-moving feeds, constant commentary and increasing mental health challenges for young women, fathers often fall into the trap of trying to repair, analyze or lecture their way through their daughters' anxieties, he suggested. 

Gallagher, who details his parenting journey in his new book "Turns Out They Were Right All Along," admits that overruling his own instincts to speak was an important step in making use of the good advice he's received over a lifetime.

"I’m a talkative guy. My career is talking," Gallagher said. "When I was younger with them, I would try to explain what I think."

Gallagher figured out that his daughters did want to hear from him.

5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

What they wanted was to simply be heard.

"So then you learn through the years, you just listen, and you nod, and you only jump in when they ask you to jump in," he said.

When daughters know their fathers are paying quiet, steady attention without rushing to judge or correct, it fosters a unique sense of security — which Gallagher has learned firsthand.

"They want to be heard, they want to get it off their chest," he said. "Instead of screaming and yelling, these girls just want to talk it out. And when requested, they want your advice — but only when requested."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Although he once dreamed of having an "all-American quarterback" son, Gallagher admitted that having girls is "the greatest thing in the world."

This active presence extends beyond daily conversations and into how fathers help their daughters build resilience against life's inevitable bumps, he said. Gallagher recalled watching his youngest daughter take a hard fall during a youth soccer match.

"I'm looking at her, and she's looking at me, and I said, 'Hey, it's all good. You know, it'll be fine,'" Gallagher recalled. "She scores a goal five minutes later, and she looks over at me.... It is soothing for them to know that somebody is really paying close attention."

This contrasts with his mother’s approach when an eight-year-old Gallagher tried to quit football. Instead of making the call for him, his mother — nicknamed "Big Red" — forced him to go to practice and tell the coach himself.

By the end of the day, Gallagher was hooked on the game, in part thanks to a coach who likely sensed his hesitation and put him straight to work.

"The first couple of weeks, it was just tackling and blocking and calisthenics and jumping jacks and push-ups, and I'm like, "Oh I hate this,'" he recalled.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"So, I'm sitting in my full pads in my mom's avocado-green recliner ... and I said [to my mother], 'I don't want to play football anymore. I want to quit.' And she said, 'Fine, go quit.'

"I walk on to the practice field and the coach looks at me, and he blows the whistle three times, and then he screams at me, 'Gallagher! You're late! Give me five laps.'"

Gallagher did as his coach said until he was instructed to get out on the field and stay quiet.

And finally, there were footballs.

"I fell in love with football and played it through college," he said. "[Coach] saw me coming from a mile away and was not about to let me quit — and my mom knew."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"And I think that today, kids need to be put in that very same position. If you want to do something, if you want to quit something, you need to do it. You need to fight your own battles."

While talent and teamwork are important for being successful in life, the fortitude to show up every day, despite challenges, is what propels most people forward, he indicated.

"You build your career, you build your character and you build your esteem. You build your confidence," he said. "Career, confidence, character."

In his new book, Gallagher drives home the message that great guidance is "so valuable to young minds." And some of the most valuable life lessons sometimes come at the most unexpected times from the most unexpected people, he said. 

"It's so good for young minds and young bodies to get good guidance, but you don't always recognize good guidance," he said. "The best lesson is that wisdom, guidance, advice — it comes at the most unexpected times."

"My advice to everybody is listen," he went on. 

"Listen to people. Hear them out. Sometimes it hits you like a sledgehammer, and sometimes it seeps in, and you don't really understand it for years. So listen."

Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

item.title: SMU vs Louisville could be a college football shootout with the over at 58.5 looking strong

Luckily, Week 2 saw me get wins and get some of that cash back, but there is still work to be done. There are quite a few tasty matchups on the docket for today’s College Football schedule. One that stands out to me is this one between SMU and Louisville.

Coming into the season, SMU was ranked 19th, and after two victories, they’ve moved up slightly to 16th. The opening game of the Mustangs’ season was not easy and was a strong challenge for them. They faced Florida State in Florida, and despite the Seminoles having struggles lately, this was still a good opponent. They alternated scores all game, but the Mustangs scored first and last, which resulted in a win for the Mustangs. They kicked a game-winning field goal with just 20 seconds remaining.

item.title: Congressman Tom Barrett: 'Being a socialist should disqualify him for people's consideration in my district'
item.description: Michigan's Tom Barrett is locked in a tight race in the Lansing-based seventh district against William Lawrence, founder of the Sunrise Movement.
item.content:encoded:
Control of Congress may very well run through Michigan's seventh district. Anchored by Lansing, the state capital, it features a large blue city, surrounded by reddish suburbs, and deep red rural areas. It is consistently described as one of the closest swing districts in the country.

Freshman Congressman Tom Barrett narrowly won the district in 2024, and is now locked in a tight race with William Lawrence, an activist and founder of the climate change-focused Sunrise Movement.

Barrett is a 21-year Army veteran helicopter pilot, who served numerous deployments overseas, before returning to Michigan and spending nearly a decade in the state legislature.

7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

The race has recently been roiled by a series of controversial social media posts. In some of them, Lawrence called the nuclear family "an isolating, violent way of organizing society" and praised campaigns to abolish the police. 

He now claims that his views have changed.

Barrett argues that the newfound shift is about political expediency, not genuine conviction:

"I think we got to take him at his word that this was his absolute true ideology and it wasn't just this one statement that he made. He made repetitive statements against police, calling to not just defund but abolish the police altogether. He wanted to throw open the borders. He said if we're a humane country, we've got to throw open the borders and redistribute all of the wealth. 

"He called the nuclear family a violent way to organize society, as you said. Countless other statements that he's made and other things that he has done that show a pattern of behavior that this is not an isolated incident. 

"And obviously it's clear to any neutral observer that he is doing this because he is running in a competitive district trying to get elected to Congress. He's not running in Rashida Tlaib's district or AOC's district where they're far more sympathetic to these DSA-aligned socialist candidates. He's running in the district that I live in where I'm raising my own nuclear family."

Barrett contends that the implementation of Lawrence's border and immigration policies would pose a clear and present danger to the safety of Americans:

"Well, the foremost obvious risk of these open border policies of my opponent is just starting with the public safety threat. So take out all of the other economic factors: just the physical threats to our communities are substantial. 

"There are criminal gang activities. We have cartels that were freely operating both ways across the border under the Biden administration. We had upwards of ten or even fifteen million illegal immigrants that came into our country completely unvetted."

Barrett also argues that the fentanyl crisis is directly tied to border and immigration policies as well.

"The leading cause of death of Americans my age wasn't cancer, wasn't heart disease, it was fentanyl overdose deaths. People that I served with in the military that came home and survived combat and died of fentanyl overdose…because of drugs that were pouring across our border. 

"For the first time in my life, we have seen a significant decline in fentanyl overdose deaths, really because of the efforts…to secure our border, and my opponent, William Lawrence, would entirely reverse that, throw the border open again, abolish the police at the same time. 

"And we can only assume the outcome of that would be far more Americans dying of fentanyl deaths, as well as gang activity and other tragic circumstances that arise when you have an open border and no public safety to protect Americans."

William Lawrence is also a longtime member of the DSA (Democratic Socialists of America), but recently claims that he let his membership lapse. Barrett argues that Lawrence remains a fervent believer in socialist ideology, but is merely trying to downplay his true beliefs to win a competitive race:

"Well, I think being a socialist should disqualify him for people's consideration in my district. You look at the tenets of socialism and what they want to do and the endorsement of that. 

MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC CANDIDATE TRIES TO JUSTIFY DELETED POSTS THAT REVEAL FAR-LEFT BELIEFS

"My opponent…cleverly claims that he let his membership lapse, I don't know, two weeks before the primary election on the eve of him winning…to face off against me in one of the most competitive congressional races in the country that will arguably decide control of the House of Representatives. 

"So he doesn't disavow the democratic socialists…He has embraced all of their positions, gathered all of their support, really benefited from the support of the democratic socialist movement. 

"And then when the time comes to defend those positions, he wants to say, well I let my membership lapse so you can't hold me accountable for all their positions. But I didn't leave under any actual disagreement with them. I'm simply leaving for political reasons because he's so focused on trying to win this election in a desperate attempt to not be accountable to his own record, but to distract away from the devastating effects of socialism and what that would mean for our country if he were to be elected."

Perhaps the most controversial of Lawrence's statements involved a post expressing frustration and outrage with politicians on climate policy. Lawrence, specifically targeting West Virginia Senator Joe Manchin, wrote: 'Hurry up and die so that we can get started."

Barrett believes that this type of rhetoric should put the voters of the seventh district on high alert:

"Obviously that's entirely inappropriate, something that should really raise the attention of every single reasonable American to say that that's not how we go about our rhetoric here in our country. Politics is a full contact sport…but I've never in my political life, in any campaign, called on political figures to 'F you and hurry up and die.' 

"And that shows the radicalization…He was a founding member of the Green New Deal Alliance in Michigan, calling to ban gasoline-powered vehicles that we build in my district that employ thousands of people in my district."

Midterm elections generally hinge on economics and affordability issues are driving the political narrative today in tight races around the country. Barrett makes the case that congressional Republicans have delivered on everyday pocketbook issues:

"Well, we lowered costs on people's taxes, certainly…and we expanded the child tax credit. We saved families taxes to the expanded standard deduction, streamlined filing for individuals. No taxes on tips, no taxes on overtime, no tax on Social Security. I wanna take that a step further and have no taxes health care. Give every American a tax-exempt health savings account and expand the things that they can use it for, for healthy groceries, gym memberships, fitness equipment.

"Obviously bring down the cost of gas as well with the conflict in Iran that I have again voted my conscience on as well and want to see gas prices come down and that will affect a lot of other parts of the economy as well around affordability. These are things that we can face. 

"But if we hand our country over to radical socialists who are simply going to tax Americans to death and then pass on benefits to illegal immigrants and people who refuse to go to work and participate in the economy. We will be worse off for that.

"So this is a very, very important election. I stand on my own merits. I know what I've done here in Congress. It's my job to go out and make the case to the voters in my district, and contrast that with the exact things that my opponent has said what he has stood for and what his pattern of behavior has shown in what he would do if he were elected to Congress."

item.title: Trinidad Chambliss leads Ole Miss Rebels offense as Lane Kiffin faces former team in SEC football spotlight
item.description: Trinidad Chambliss and Kewan Lacy power Ole Miss against Lane Kiffin's LSU Tigers in an SEC rivalry game loaded with storylines and emotion.
item.content:encoded:
Gee, I wish there were some storylines for this game between the LSU Tigers and the Ole Miss Rebels. There isn’t going to be a game this week that has more attention than this one. I’m excited to see what happens with the crowd as much as I am on the field. The product on the field should be one of the best games of the weekend as well.

The LSU Tigers are off to a good start and are currently ranked at 7th in the nation. The main story you’ll hear about is Lane Kiffin, and I feel like I should share my opinion. Lane Kiffin leaving Ole Miss for LSU is… not a big deal. Everyone in the world has goals and desires, and outside of a family business, you're going to work for a competitor if they are paying you more or have a better reputation. That is exactly what you should do. People will get over it, but we all knew this would be a major story this week, and probably much of the season.

As for the actual players of this game, it has been a good start against bad teams for the Tigers. They blew out Clemson 51-10 in their first game, and in the second, they took down Louisiana Tech by a final score of 45-14. I’ve got some questions about how much of a leash Sam Leavitt has after throwing four interceptions compared to two touchdowns in his two games.

ELLA LANGLEY, DISTRACTIONS AND LANE KIFFIN: PETE GOLDING CALLS OLE MISS-LSU ‘HIGH SCHOOL HOMECOMING’

Ole Miss really shouldn’t feel bad about Kiffin leaving, and so far, they’ve done everything you need to do to make a team and school forget about him. They are 2-0 for the season, winning over one quality opponent and one easier one. Their season opener was against Louisville, and they took them down 41-38 in Week 1. Last week, they beat Charlotte with a final score of 41-9. That was a much more comfortable win, obviously.

All eyes tonight will be on quarterback Trinidad Chambliss. He was a key piece of Kiffin’s success at Ole Miss last year. After a court battle giving him eligibility, Chambliss has looked good, going 44-for-62 so far with five touchdowns and one interception. I’ve been impressed with their work on the ground as well. Half of the carries have gone to Kewan Lacy, and he has 148 yards and three touchdowns.

I think the biggest question about this game is which one will get the stop when they need it. The game opened somewhat as a pick’em, but has moved in favor of the Tigers taking this one. I do think this will be a very hostile environment for LSU to play in. I also have been really unimpressed with Leavitt. I’m taking the points here, and I do think Ole Miss can win this game outright. Give me the Rebels +3.

item.title: The week Gainesville forgot about football: Inside the terror that gripped Florida during the 1990 murders
item.description: UF alumni recall the terror of Danny Rolling's 1990 murder spree and how Steve Spurrier's home opener against Oklahoma State restored normalcy.
item.content:encoded:
College football season in Gainesville is everything.

Everything.

The town has forever revolved around the Florida Gators. Gainesville is a college town. It's built around the university. As the program goes, so does the town.

With all due respect to Miami and FSU, most would argue that Florida is a Gators state. Yes, I know that'll ruffle some feathers. Let's not get caught up on that, please. Just bear with me.

My point? Very few things in life can actually take attention away from the Florida Gators during football season — especially with a legend like Steve Spurrier set to return home, this time as the program's head coach.

August of 1990 did just that.

HOW A PODCAST COMMUNITY HELPED RESTORE THE CONTROVERSIAL 'GATOR BAIT' CHANT FOR FLORIDA FOOTBALL TEAM

"I remember at Walmart, the gun line was down the aisle," former UF student Erik Tallbacka told OutKick this week. "When a hurricane's coming, and you're at Home Depot and preparing, there's that kind of electricity, like something's coming. And it was that hurricane sensation.

"But it wasn't a hurricane's coming. It was people getting killed every night, for three nights in a row. The whole campus, the whole town, just had that palpable feeling of 'everybody's in this together.'"

Earlier this week, I wrote about ESPN's recent 30 for 30 on Danny Rolling, also known as the "Gainesville Ripper." Rolling brutally murdered five students in August 1990 — days before Labor Day weekend and roughly two weeks before the start of a new football season.

Rolling was eventually arrested, pled guilty to the murders — along with several in Shreveport, Louisiana — and was later sentenced to death. He died via lethal injection in 2006.

Rolling became known as the "Gainesville Ripper." His killing spree, which had no real motive, led to several books, and one movie. The horror franchise "Scream" is loosely based on the Gainesville Murders, according to the screenwriter Kevin Williamson.

So, yes — 36 years later, that infamous week is still fresh one everyone's minds. You don't simply live through that and forget, you know?

I had dozens of readers reach out to me after I wrote about it on Wednesday — most of them UF alumni who were on campus while Rolling was at large.

The word they all used? Horrific.

"You could drive down the road or through apartment complexes and people had braces in their windows to keep someone from opening them," remembered Duane Engel. "No one had any clue who was involved."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Of course, there was no social media, either. This was decades before X. Tallbacka said you watched the nightly news for any new information, and that was all you got.

Everyone was on edge.

"As you walked around town and campus, I remember, if you're going into a store, just looking at everybody, like it could be any guy," he recalled. "And we just had no idea. When you'd go to bed at night, especially by the third day, when there'd been five murders, I mean, that night, you're wondering, is somebody going to break into my apartment?

"And so sleeping was weird. I was living with a couple other guys, my girlfriend was living with a couple girls, and we were sleeping over there. And like I mentioned, we didn't have guns. I was a big hunter, but didn't have any guns in college. But we had brought golf clubs and baseball bats and we were sleeping on the couch. Any noise that you heard, you know, a car door slamming, you were just so on edge."

Spurrier famously allowed the girlfriends of players to sleep in Yon Hall — a high-security complex where the entire football team lived.

Matt Sovic had just returned to campus for his senior year, and attended a party the weekend the murders began. He was staying with friends at Williamsburg Village — the same complex where freshmen Sonja Larson and Christina Powell lived.

"I parked my car directly in front of the of the door to the four units that contained the residence of the first victims," he said. "As we left to go party that Saturday night, when my old roommate entered my car he tossed his beer can out of my window and into the yard.

"The next day we watched as it was placed into an evidence bag. I can guarantee you that beer in the evidence bag was a tall boy Budweiser. Not knowing yet there was a double murder, we jokingly told our friend he was a suspect for whatever happened now that they had his prints."

Rolling murdered five students from Aug. 24 to Aug. 27. Four of them were females with brunette hair and brown eyes, the same as his mother.

The fifth was 23-year-old Manny Taboada — a 6-foot-2, 200-pound male.

"It wasn’t until we found out he killed that massive guy, who worked on the corner of Acher and I think 34th, that all the egos took a fall on campus," remembered Kevin Letize, who was just starting his senior year. "We all thought it was a typical perv killer until that came out.

"Once the big kid was killed, all the 'tough' students took it much more seriously."

So, how does football fit into all of this? Well, it really doesn't — beyond, perhaps, a much-needed bookend to the most terrifying week in the history of the town.

After much discussion, Florida, and Spurrier, kicked off the new season Sept. 8 against Oklahoma State. The murders had stopped, at least for a few days, but a lot of students had left for good by then. The ones who stayed did their best to get back to some sort of normalcy.

The Gators won, 50-7. Shane Matthews instantly became a household name. Spurrier had revived Florida football. More importantly, the team had revived a town in desperate need of a reason to smile.

"I've never seen a place so terrorized," said Glenn Summers.

Added Tallbacka: "I guess everybody was in a fog. But I think by the time that game happened, it had been over a week since anybody been killed. And I do think, in retrospect, watching that game brought everybody back to normalcy. It wasn't just going to class and classes are canceled. And every night for three nights, somebody has been killed.

"By the time a week went by, by the time the football game happened, I think that must have been when everybody finally relaxed. I think that was the conclusion."

item.title: John Ritter's widow Amy Yasbeck details the fatal misdiagnosis she says led to his death
item.description: Amy Yasbeck reveals John Ritter was misdiagnosed with a heart attack the night he died, when a CT scan could have detected his aortic dissection.
item.content:encoded:
John Ritter's widow Amy Yasbeck is opening up about the actor's final hours more than two decades after his death.

In September 2003, Ritter died at the age of 54 after suffering an acute aortic dissection, a tear in the inner layer of the aorta, the body's largest artery that delivers blood away from the heart.

Ahead of Aortic Dissection Awareness Week and what would have been Ritter's 78th birthday on Sept. 17, Yasbeck, who founded the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health, and the actor's son, Tyler Ritter, who serves on its board, joined Fox News Digital for an interview.

CARLY PEARCE SAYS HEART CONDITION LEFT HER FEARING A HEART ATTACK: ‘IS MY HEART OK?’

Looking back on her husband's death, Yasbeck recalled how Ritter was mistakenly treated for a heart attack after arriving at the hospital, which she said "led to what eventually happened."

"John was sadly misdiagnosed on the night he passed away," Yasbeck said.

"And they didn't do any imaging, but he looked like the guy — right age, right weight, everything — to have a heart attack, and he had chest pain," she continued. "So they just started loading him up with blood thinners and stuff."

"And this is sad because it was the opposite. It wasn't a block in his heart, it was a tear in his aorta, so everything they did that night led to what eventually happened," Yasbeck said. "Because there are ways, once it starts dissecting, if you get to the hospital in time, your chances are way better of living."

Following Ritter's death, Yasbeck filed a wrongful death lawsuit alleging Ritter's aortic dissection was misdiagnosed. In 2008, a jury found in favor of the two physicians remaining in the case.

WATCH: JOHN RITTER'S DEATH HIT SO HARD BECAUSE ‘YOU FELT LIKE YOU KNEW HIM’: FOUNDATION CEO

To mark Aortic Dissection Awareness Week, which runs from Sept. 13 to 19, the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health, is launching its "50 for 50" campaign, encouraging supporters to donate $50 while drawing attention to the fact that up to 50% of people who suffer an aortic dissection die before reaching medical care.

Yasbeck told Fox News Digital that she believes annual estimates of aortic dissections likely undercount the number of cases because patients who die before arriving at a hospital often are not included in the data. She said that improving awareness of the condition is one of the most effective ways to reduce those deaths.

However, Yasbeck emphasized that raising awareness is not just for patients and families. She pointed out the importance of ensuring doctors recognize that chest pain can signal an aortic dissection, not just a heart attack.

COUNTRY STAR ASHLEY COOKE SPEAKS OUT ABOUT RARE HEART CONDITION THAT COULD END HER LIFE AT ANY MOMENT

"Your heart can be in perfect shape," she said. "You can be an athlete."

"And if the blood that's being pumped into your aorta is going inside the layers of the aorta, instead of being traveled to all of the rest of the highway where it's supposed to go, it's curtains for you," she continued.

"So it's so important to be able to have that awareness," Yasbeck added. "And there's no drug for aortic dissection at this point in time. For blood pressure, which sometimes can help you if you are at risk, right? Keep your blood pressure down, but there's no instant fix for it. You have to be a participant in your own health in this regard. And by doing that, you are also protecting your family. For generations, actually."

Yasbeck said she recently witnessed firsthand how her husband's story has become part of emergency medicine. She recalled accompanying a friend with chest pain to the hospital where medical staff told her they were ordering a CT scan to check for "the John Ritter thing" to rule out an aortic dissection.

"They said, 'We're checking for the John Ritter thing', not knowing who I am, not knowing whom my friend is that was a friend of John's," she remembered. "It was just like this relief came over me. And my buddy, you know, gave me the thumbs up."

"The fact that they said checking for that ‘John Ritter thing,’ talking shorthand to me, I freaking love that. Call it whatever you want. CT scan, a CAT scan, is the gold standard for diagnosing in an emergency situation, in any situation, but to be able to realize as soon as you can, ‘This is not a heart attack. This is an aortic dissection,’" she continued. "'Fix this a whole different way.'"

'GAME OF THRONES' STAR EMILIA CLARKE WAS CONVINCED SHE 'CHEATED DEATH' AFTER SURVIVING TWO BRAIN ANEURYSMS

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Yasbeck shared that doctors and researchers had told her for years that Ritter's death marked a turning point in awareness of aortic dissection.

"There was kind of a pre-John Ritter awareness of aortic dissection and a post," she said. "Sadly, John died in the last hours of pre-John Ritter awareness."

WATCH: JOHN RITTER'S LEGACY IS HELPING PREVENT DEADY AORTIC DISSECTIONS, DOCTOR SAYS

Since Ritter's death, the "Three's Company" star's family has worked through the John Ritter Foundation for Aortic Health to raise awareness about thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections. A thoracic aortic aneurysm is an enlargement of the body's main artery that can often be detected through screening before it tears into an aortic dissection, a life-threatening emergency.

Ritter's widow and his children have encouraged people to learn about their family medical history and seek appropriate screening when they are at increased risk because thoracic aortic aneurysms and dissections can have a genetic component.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Yasbeck said doctors now believe Ritter's father likely died from an undiagnosed aortic dissection, while routine screenings after his death revealed the same condition in his brother Tom, allowing him to undergo life-saving surgery before it became fatal.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Tyler, 41, told Fox News Digital that becoming aware of his family history in the aftermath of his father's death had changed his approach to his own health. Ritter shared Tyler as well as son Jason Ritter, 46, and daughter Carly Ritter, 44, with his first wife, actress Nancy Morgan. Yasbeck, who was Ritter's second wife, shared son Noah Ritter, 28.

"It's impossible not to imagine that there's a parallel universe where the family demanded an autopsy on our grandfather and discovered an aortic dissection, which led to my dad and his brother getting screened," Tyler said. "And as we see with Tommy, as Amy just said, Tommy is still alive and doing great."

"It's just too easy to imagine that in this other universe, where my grandfather was properly diagnosed, that my dad would be totally fine right now with just an aortic replacement surgery," he continued. "And that, on the one hand, is very difficult to accept and to comprehend."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"On the other hand, it has provided a massive silver lining," Tyler added. "I get scanned every year. My kids know I get scanned. They know why I get scanned. They know that my dad was the last one in our family. Our mission is that he is the last in our family to suffer a dissection."

Tyler said watching his own children discover their grandfather through episodes of "Three's Company" has reinforced the importance of preserving Ritter's legacy through awareness.

He explained that though aneurysms are often asymptomatic, they can be detected through screening, which is why he encourages families with a history of aortic disease or unexplained early deaths to speak with their doctors.

WATCH: JOHN RITTER FOUNDATION CEO RECALLS SURVIVING LIFE-THREATENING AORTIC DISSECTION

"The more you know," he said. "If you can spot in a first-degree relative that there's a potential for a missed or undiagnosed illness or disease, it would just be worth asking your doctor."

Looking back, Tyler said his father's death remains a tragedy, but one that has helped protect other families.

"It is unfortunate. It's a tragedy," he said. "But it has happened. And as a result, there are just countless numbers of lives that have been saved."

item.title: Strange rock catches scientist's eye during creek search, leading to rare discovery
item.description: An Ice Age Pacific mastodon molar in immaculate condition was found in a San Mateo County creek, and scientists say the rest of the skeleton may still be buried there.
item.content:encoded:
A scientist surveying a California creek recently stumbled across something unexpected: a tooth from the mouth of an Ice Age giant.

The discovery of the tooth, which belonged to an ancient Pacific mastodon, was announced by the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) in San Mateo County, California.

Mastodons were massive, elephant-like herbivores that went extinct roughly 11,700 years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age.

SHOCKING PREHISTORIC DISCOVERY ON NJ BEACH '100%' CAME FROM COLOSSAL ANCIENT PREDATOR

The tooth was found in a Midpen preserve creek by Brigid Lynch, a Balance Hydrologics geomorphologist who was surveying the area as part of an effort to improve the habitat of the threatened California red-legged frog.

"As a geologist, I've gone out and seen stuff in the field, but definitely nothing as exciting as this," Lynch said in a release.

Pictures of the molar show its strange shape, which Lynch initially thought was an oddly shaped rock.

The tooth is in "immaculate condition," Wayne Thompson, CEO of Pacific Paleontology, told Fox News Digital in an interview. 

T REX FOOTPRINTS UNEARTHED IN FIRST-EVER DISCOVERY 66 MILLION YEARS AFTER CREATURE WALKED THE EARTH

Thompson, whose job it was to examine the fossil and assess the site where it was discovered, said the tooth likely dates back between 50,000 and 100,000 years, based on where it was found.

"There is a lot of misinformation going around about the age of the tooth," he said. "Most of the reports out [there] are saying it's 10,000 years old, but it's not 10,000 years.

"From the location where the specimen was found, we can pretty confidently say that it’s much, much older than 11,700 years — probably on the order between 50 and 100,000 years," he added.

ANCIENT OCEAN MYSTERY DEEPENS AS LONG-MISIDENTIFIED FOSSIL IS FINALLY REVEALED BY RESEARCHERS

Thompson said the condition of the tooth also offers clues about what happened to it after the mastodon died, noting that it "hadn't moved very much in the stream where the creature died."

"Mastodon teeth are — the roots are extremely fragile — and this one had the majority of the roots of the molar still preserved with it intact, and so, it wasn't tumbled around in the stream," he said.

The paleontologist believes the rest of the animal may still be at the site.

"It probably recently came out of the skull and the skull, along with the rest of the bones, are still buried out there," he said.

It is "extremely rare" to find a mastodon molar in such well-preserved condition, Thompson said.

"It doesn't happen often. ... [It's] quite uncommon," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Looking ahead, researchers from Stanford University's Doerr School of Sustainability plan to carbon date the molar to determine its exact age.

Researchers will also create a 3-D scan of the tooth, which will be used to produce a replica.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Thompson said mastodons favored creek and river valleys, browsing on leaves rather than grazing on grasses as mammoths did.

Alder trees, he said, were among their preferred food sources — and they still line the creek where the tooth was found.

"Even today, when we went out to the site to inspect where the biological monitor was surveying, there were still hundreds of alders along the stream," Thompson said.

item.title: 'Resident Evil' Review: Director Zach Cregger delivers infectious reboot to gory video game franchise
item.description: Fox News Digital reviews Sony Pictures' "Resident Evil" starring Austin Abrams, Paul Walter Hauser, Kali Reis and Zach Cherry. Directed by Zach Cregger.
item.content:encoded:
Zach Cregger might not be your cup of tea, but his incredible gift behind the camera cannot be ignored. 

The writer/director comes armed with absolute terror and hilarity, two things that seem incompatible on the surface, yet he's able to blend seamlessly.  

And his latest horror film, "Resident Evil," is no different. 

BOX OFFICE COMEBACK: HOW SUMMER 2026 OFFERS A GLIMMER OF HOPE FOR HOLLYWOOD IN THE POST-COVID ERA

If "Resident Evil" sounds familiar, that's because it's a long-running video game franchise that turned into a long-running movie franchise starring Milla Jovovich. 

In this version of "Resident Evil," her character Alice is nowhere to be found. Instead, it stars Austin Abrams, who plays a medical courier named Bryan urgently tasked with delivering what he believes is a vital organ to a hospital in Raccoon City.

'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN

What was supposed to be a quiet, uneventful drive devolves into a series of unfortunate events for Bryan, the cause of which stems from a lab leak of a virus (we all know how easily this can happen, right?) developed by the Umbrella Corporation that transforms organisms into what can only be described as ungodly monsters from the darkest of nightmares.

The "Resident Evil" movies we've been used to feature Jovovich being a gun-slinging badass with a zombie body count in the thousands. Here, the scrawny Bryan can barely figure out how to turn the safety off. He's not your knight in shining armor — in fact, he's kind of an idiot. Yet, there's something endearing and relatable about him. 

It was a bold choice for Cregger to cast Abrams as Bryan. You may recognize Abrams for his stints in "Euphoria" and "This Is Us" or various movies, like Cregger's 2025 Oscar-winning breakout "Weapons," but he hasn't been the star of such a high-profile project, particularly as big as this. His performance is able to generate big laughs as he maintains such seriousness (after all, Bryan is literally fighting for survival). "Resident Evil" should hopefully mark a new chapter in Abrams' career as a leading man — because he's certainly capable.

Abrams is essentially a one-man show, but Paul Walter Hauser ("Richard Jewell," "I, Tonya"), Kali Reis ("True Detective") and Zach Cherry ("Severance") make memorable, albeit brief, appearances.

‘MUTINY’ REVIEW: JASON STATHAM TAKES NO PRISONERS IN MINDLESS BUT AMUSING BRAWLER FLICK ON THE HIGH SEAS

As a fan of the original source material, Cregger brings the video game experience to life, playing around with first-person angles as we see from Bryan's view of where he's aiming his gun, or the tracking shot as we follow him in the snowy terrain or an eerily quiet house. He and co-writer Shay Hatten (who wrote the more recent "John Wick" installments) were able to stick the landing by juggling bloody thrills with gallows humor. 

And no offense to Cregger's franchise predecessor Paul W.S. Anderson, but the production value is just far superior in this "Resident Evil" between the cinematography from Oscar nominee Dariusz Wolski ("The Martian"), the score from brothers Hays and Ryan Holladay and the editing from Joe Murphy (all of whom worked on "Weapons" and Cregger's solo feature debut "Barbarian") as well as the gruesome special effects and makeup work. 

‘THE END OF OAK STREET’ REVIEW: ANNE HATHAWAY, EWAN MCGREGOR FIGHT DINOSAURS IN SURPRISINGLY FUN MOVIE

While it's difficult to rank this higher than "Barbarian" and "Weapons" ("Barbarian" is still my favorite of the three), Cregger is flexing his muscles taking on a Hollywood franchise and has cemented his status among the small elite group of rising filmmakers who have had such a strong streak so early in their careers (think Jordan Peele or Yorgos Lanthimos). And if he keeps it up, perhaps he can reach Christopher Nolan's status where audiences flock to see his movies because the man in the director's chair has become the real star. 

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

"Resident Evil" comes back to life in this fun, infectious reboot thanks to Zach Cregger's brilliance behind the camera and Austin Abrams' charming performance as an unlikely lead in front of it. If you can't stomach the gore, this isn't for you. But for those who get a kick out of it, get that bucket of popcorn ready.

"Resident Evil" is rated R for strong bloody violence, gore and language throughout. Running time: 1 hour, 30 minutes. In theaters now.

item.title: Former ESPN anchor smears Caitlin Clark fans with sweeping, false accusations of racism | Matt Calkins
item.description: Cari Champion called Caitlin Clark an "avatar" for hate and her fans MAGA on podcasts with Jemele Hill and Bakari Sellers, sparking fierce debate.
item.content:encoded:
Did you know that Caitlin Clark is an "avatar for people who want to spread hate"?

Because Cari Champion does.

Did you know that the fans who latched onto her are just middle Americans "who want to see White women do well in a sport that's traditionally Black"?

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Champion's all over that, too.

The former ESPN anchor would also like you to know that Clark hasn't done enough to give Black players their respect, and that the WNBA is coddling Caitlin and her "MAGA" fans to the detriment of the league.

She shared these insights in separate podcasts with Jemele Hill and Bakari Sellers. It was all very enlightening.

And by enlightening I mean ridiculous.

No doubt that Clark — the most popular women's basketball player ever — has displayed traits that warrant criticism. She can be petulant. She can be hostile toward refs. And she's about to lead the league in turnovers for the third consecutive season.

But the racial narratives the media manufactures with her are as absurd as the maligning of her fan base. Who's really the hateful one here?

Let's start with Champion's notion that Clark's fans are essentially country bumpkins looking for a white face to cheer for. This makes no sense. Sue Bird, Dianna Taurasi, Breanna Stewart, Sabrina Ionescu, and Kelsey Plum were all No. 1 overall picks who won the Wooden Award in their final year of college. All White — but none were selling out arenas.

ELLE DUNCAN BLAMES CAITLIN CLARK, HER FANS FOR MEDIA SMEAR CAMPAIGN WHILE IGNORING FACTS

That's because they weren't pulling up from 28 feet ten times a game en route to setting the all-time NCAA scoring record while leading the country in assists for three straight years. Clark didn't rise to fame because she played college basketball unlike any woman who's come before her, she did it because she played college hoops unlike any person had before. Given how popular athletes such as Serena Williams and Simone Biles were, it seems silly to think Clark wouldn't have achieved the same notoriety if she were Black.

Plus, wasn't it LeBron James who posted "if you don't rock with Caitlin Clark's game you're just a FLAT OUT HATER!!!!!"? And isn't it Tyrese Haliburton who's a courtside regular at her Fever games? Could just be me, but those guys don't look very White.

Next, there is Champion's assertion that Clark's fans are trying to "spread hate." Or that the league looks the other way when this "entitled" and "nasty" fan base "behaves like MAGA." She went so far as to say that Clark supporters can't accept other players' "queerness" or "blackness."

Really?

The source Clark detractors always cite is online vitriol, and there's no doubt that exists. But such vitriol never seems to be quantified in a way that's comparable to other famous athletes' fan bases. The unfortunate truth is that there are always going to be internet trolls who want to denigrate people behind their cat avatar on X. But are there any examples in which Clark fans crossed the line from online noise into real-world harassment?

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

In 2024, Brittney Griner said "I don’t appreciate the new fans that sit there and yell racial slurs at myself, my teammates and the people that I play against." But she provided no specifics or evidence to substantiate the claim, and though she didn’t single out Fever fans as the culprits, there was a strong implication that they were. Similarly, in May of last year, Angel Reese claimed that Fever fans hurled racist comments her way during a game. But after a review involving fans, team and arena staff and audio and video from the game, the WNBA said it could not substantiate the allegation. Does this mean it never happened? Not necessarily.

But concrete evidence of Clark fans acting in a hateful manner — at least in real time — is severely lacking.

What's not lacking, however, is the hostility toward Clark and her fans. Champion said that Clark being heterosexual, White and Catholic helped bring a new fan base that the WNBA is "coddling" for the sake of business. First of all, Clark being the most entertaining women's basketball player in the world is what brought in all those new fans — but could you imagine the inverse of that statement? That if a broadcaster bemoaned the "coddling" of a gay, Black and Muslim fan base? Instant cancellation.

But Champion goes on. And she seems to disapprove of Clark not going out of her way to highlight Black players in a league that is 70 percent Black. She wishes Caitlin could be more like Wings point guard Paige Bueckers, who, in her 2021 ESPY's speech, said that Black women's basketball players were being overlooked. OK. Two things.

1)Every women's basketball player was being overlooked before Clark came on the scene. Her arrival elevated the popularity of players Black and White alike. 2) Could you imagine if a pundit said that Tiger Woods should do more to highlight his white peers in a white-dominated sport? Or that Shohei Ohtani should thank all the white players that came before him? Outrage would justifiably ensue. So let's stop with that idea.

Sports leagues are not built on color. They are built on talent. Saying white players such as Clark or Bueckers should pay homage to their Black peers is as absurd as saying Steph Curry and Jalen Brunson should pay homage to their tall peers. It's about the individual.

And if we're being honest here, Clark's race and sexual orientation may very well be working against her. Last year, after being called for a foul involving Clark, Griner was caught on camera saying what appeared to be "trash, f---ing White girl." Then, there was this year's All-Star voting, where Caitlin was ranked second among guards by the fans, third by the media....and 11th by the players. One might say this was pure jealousy, except that Kelsey Plum, who is also white and straight, finished sixth among fans, fifth among media and 12th among players. The year before, it went 6-6-16 for Plum.

Most of us who follow Clark are aware of the hits she takes on the court, whether it's Chennedy Carter hip-checking her to the ground or Alyssa Thomas making closed-fist contact with her throat. But the hits are just as blatant from within press boxes or studios — and it's fair to question people's motivation.

No one here is saying Caitlin or her supporters are above criticism. But all of Champion's rhetoric about Clark and her supposedly bigoted fan base?

Some might see it as provocation. I can't help but wonder if it's projection.

item.title: Deprogrammed: Former DSA insider reveals ‘frightening’ socialist agenda drove him from ‘extreme’ ideology
item.description: Jake Altman, a former DSA executive board member, reveals how the Democratic Socialists of America silenced dissent and defended the Maduro regime.

Jake Altman, a former executive board member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in Boston, is sounding the alarm about the organization’s efforts to "force their agenda down other people's throats."

"I had been involved in my local union and met some people who were far, far to the left, in like, a frightening way. I was looking for a more pragmatic and thoughtful option on the left that was focused on economic policy," Altman told Fox News Digital.

"One of the concerns I had very quickly was that [the] DSA was beginning to sound more and more like those extreme groups on the left that I, you know, certainly didn't want anything to do with," he continued.

FORMER DSA MEMBER ALLEGES COMMUNISTS HAVE ‘CAPTURED’ SOCIALIST GROUP, WARNS DEMOCRATIC PARTY IS NEXT

Altman went on to recall an incident in 2017 that raised his concerns, when the DSA elected longtime Austin, Texas, activist Danny Fetonte to its National Political Committee.

A few weeks after his election, Fetonte "abruptly resigned from his position at DSA, and encouraged others to question their membership with the group."

His departure from the organization came after the DSA found that Fetonte had worked for the Combined Law Enforcement Associations of Texas (CLEAT) — a police union — and a reality that Altman called "troubling."

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ERUPT OVER 2028 ENDORSEMENT AS AOC SPECULATION GROWS: 'DANGEROUS PATH'

The former DSA leader recalled voicing concern in 2019 after the DSA issued a statement that he characterized as "defending or apologizing for the Maduro regime."

"I raised a concern about that … and I said, DSA should be denouncing Maduro … the Democratic socialists and social Democrats in Venezuela are in the opposition — there should be free and fair elections," he continued.

"The person disagreed with me and defended, you know, essentially defended the Maduro regime," Altman revealed.

WAR ERUPTS ON FAR LEFT AS DSA ENDORSES CHALLENGER AGAINST SITTING HOUSE PROGRESSIVE

"Flash forward to today … you have DSA members saying, Bernie Sanders, AOC, they're not socialists," Altman relayed.

"In [the] DSA right now, you've seen a marriage between more traditional Marxist utopianism and what you might call third worldism … boiling it down [it’s] this view that America is a unique evil in the world and that its enemies have a point," he said.

"I personally think that just given the organization and the structure inside, that a lot of dissident voices have been silenced. A lot of dissident voices have left the organization. My advice would be [to] leave," Altman said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Lawyer says 250-foot Trump arch disrupts historic sightlines cherished by veterans seeking burial at Arlington
item.description: Three Vietnam veterans are suing to block Trump's Great Triumphal Arch, saying it would destroy iconic views near Arlington National Cemetery.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C.—which he said would be the largest in the world—is being opposed by three Vietnam veterans who say the project would block views between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery, and Arlington House, some of the most well-known views in and around the city.

Veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, and Jon Gundersen—along with architectural historian Calder Loth—have been engaged in a months-long legal battle with the Trump administration over the "Great Triumphal Arch".

"Our plaintiffs are three Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian. All of them have a deep personal relationship with Arlington National Cemetery," Nicolas Sansone, an attorney with the Public Citizen Litigation Group representing the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital. "Two of our veteran plaintiffs hope to be buried there."

DEMS UNLOAD ON TRUMP’S LATEST DC UPDATE WITH ‘CHRISTIAN NATIONALIST’ BROADSIDE, LEGAL PUSH

Trump has said the arch should be built near Arlington National Cemetery, which serves as the final resting place for more than 400,000 military service members.

Critics of the project contend that the planned structure is disrespectful to the solemn character of the cemetery. In addition, the Trump administration acknowledged in a planning document that the project will have "adverse effects on historic properties".

"Such adverse effects cannot be fully avoided while retaining the location-dependent purpose of the undertaking," the National Park Service wrote in the document.

The nation's capital was designed to keep historic landmarks from being obscured by other structures, Sansone said.

LINCOLN MEMORIAL'S HIDDEN 15,000-SQUARE-FOOT UNDERCROFT OPENS TO THE PUBLIC AFTER A CENTURY UNDERGROUND

"One of the sort of central design features is that the capital has been laid out in a very deliberate way to create this uninterrupted view between the Lincoln Memorial on the east side of the Potomac River and Arlington House, the Robert E. Lee Memorial, on the west side in Arlington National Cemetery," he said.

"So our plaintiffs… are really sort of concerned about the impact that this sort of enormous structure is going to have on that sort of historic symbolic view that each of them finds really meaningful," he added.

GOLDEN EAGLES, LIONS AND A WINGED LADY LIBERTY TOP TRUMP'S PROPOSED 250-FOOT DC TRIUMPHAL ARCH DESIGNS

Earlier this month, the administration announced that excavation work for the project would begin within the next two weeks.

The plaintiffs have asked a federal judge to issue a temporary restraining order to keep the project from moving forward, saying it can't be built without authorization from Congress.

TRUMP SIGNS ACT CLEARING THE WAY FOR MEDAL OF HONOR MONUMENT ON NATIONAL MALL

The Trump administration has cited a 1925 law that originally authorized a pair of 166-foot columns in Washington, D.C., that were never built.

Administration officials argue that past congressional approval grandfathers the triumphal arch project and allows them to avoid authorization from Congress.

"The idea is that really it's just an institutional question of who gets to decide: Is it one person, the person sitting in the White House, or should it be a sort of democratic deliberative process to sort of figure out what these monuments should look like, where they should be situated, what they should commemorate, and the like," Sansone said.

"Congress's authorization to have a particular project built at a particular time subject to a specific price cap by a now-disbanded commission can't reasonably be relied on to authorize a totally different independent project that's going to cost way more money centuries into the future," he added.

item.title: Women turn to testosterone for low sex drive as doctors confront treatment ‘experimentation’
item.description: Dr. Kudzai Dombo reveals the insurance denials and dosing guesswork women face seeking testosterone therapy as FDA regulators weigh new access.
item.content:encoded:
When women ask their doctors about taking testosterone to help with menopause symptoms, they can run into insurance rejections, confusing workarounds and dosing guesswork, as no testosterone product is FDA-approved for women in the U.S.

On Thursday, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) convened a public workshop to examine the evidence, safety and research gaps surrounding testosterone therapy for menopausal women.

Interest in testosterone therapy has grown as more women seek treatment for symptoms such as low sexual desire, fatigue and reduced quality of life during menopause — yet the lack of an FDA-approved product has left physicians relying on off-label prescribing and compounded formulations.

MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

Dr. Kudzai Dombo, a board-certified obstetrician-gynecologist, Menopause Society-certified practitioner, and prescribing physician at Alloy Health, said she sees this dynamic playing out daily in her own Los Angeles practice.

Once patients get settled on standard estrogen and progesterone regimens, "The immediate next question is, do I need testosterone?" Dombo told Fox News Digital.

Although women may hear about a wide range of potential benefits on social media and from friends, current evidence-based guidelines support testosterone therapy for only one indication: hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), or persistently low sexual desire.

Clinical evidence supporting its use for energy, mood, bone health or sleep remains limited — though many patients are eager to try it for those secondary benefits, according to Dombo.

Because no female-specific formulation exists, doctors must navigate off-label workarounds. They typically choose between using custom compounding pharmacies or micro-dosing FDA-approved male gel packets, which patients must carefully measure out at home.

ALZHEIMER'S RISK MAY BE 35% LOWER WITH COMMON MENOPAUSE TREATMENT, STUDY FINDS

This lack of standardized options creates administrative and financial hurdles. Because the therapy is off-label, insurance routinely denies coverage, forcing clinicians and patients to improvise — a frustration that Dombo experienced firsthand.

"When I was prescribed testosterone, my insurance denied coverage, and my physician recommended a compounded cream to avoid the administrative burden," Dombo recalled. "I said, 'Well, I've already tried compounded and I actually want to try the gel.'"

Using a discount coupon, she paid out of pocket and discovered that a 10-month supply of male gel packets was actually cheaper than a single month of compounded cream.

"It's just an example, I think, of how we have to adapt to a system that has not supported patients when it comes to access to testosterone therapy," she said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Dosing male products can also present clinical challenges. Dombo described a patient in her private practice who precisely measured out one-tenth of a male gel packet daily using a syringe.

Despite three months of consistency, follow-up bloodwork showed no change in hormone levels, and the patient experienced no symptom relief.

"We're left to kind of decide, 'Well, what now?'" Dombo said. "It's all experimentation ... We don't have a set guideline for how to be able to do this for women. We have to rely on the art of medicine."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The latest federal meeting represents a critical step forward, according to Dombo, who believes grassroots advocacy from patients and clinicians is forcing regulatory action.

"We're not going to stop knocking on the door, because there are several of us who believe that women deserve to be able to have access to just what they need," she said.

"Sexual health is part of your entire health," Dombo emphasized, expressing optimism that regulatory agencies will eventually adapt to support safer, standardized access.

item.title: NEWT GINGRICH: Xi is coming to Washington. He should bring one unexpected guest
item.description: Jimmy Lai's release could reset U.S.-China relations as Xi Jinping prepares to meet Trump in Washington with a business delegation next week.

When Chinese President Xi Jinping comes to Washington to meet with President Donald J. Trump next week, the agenda will be crowded.

The two men will talk trade, artificial intelligence, investment and international competition — and ultimately the future of the world’s most important bilateral relationship.

Reports indicate Xi is preparing to bring a substantial delegation of Chinese business executives with him — a sign of China’s interest in strengthening ties with America. No doubt, Xi wants President Trump to reduce tariffs on Chinese goods and ease other trade restrictions that are throttling China’s economy.

WHAT XI WANTS FROM TRUMP AS BEIJING SEEKS LEVERAGE IN HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT

PRESIDENT TRUMP REVEALS XI JINPING'S RESPONSE TO POSSIBLY RELEASING IMPRISONED CHINESE CRITIC JIMMY LAI

Lai is 78 years old. He is a British Catholic, newspaper publisher and longtime advocate of democracy in Hong Kong. In December 2025, a Hong Kong court convicted him of national security and sedition offenses (which were based on a ludicrous, draconian Chinese security law). On Feb. 9, he was sentenced to 20 years in prison. For a man of his age, this is effectively a life sentence.

Lai’s detention was clearly an example of the Chinese Communist Party seeking to silence public dissent in Hong Kong. It was nearly universally rejected by the Western world.

President Trump has been calling for Lai’s release since he campaigned in 2024. He reportedly brought it up again with Xi when they met in May, telling reporters prior to the meeting that "[Lai] tried to do the right thing. He wasn't successful. Went to jail, and people would like him out. And I'd like to see him get out, too. So, I'll bring him up again. I have brought him up."

TRUMP LEAVES CHINA WITH BREAKTHROUGHS — AND UNFINISHED BUSINESS ON XI’S BIGGEST FIGHTS

In addition to President Trump’s disapproval of Lai’s incarceration, the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for his immediate release. Other governments, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and other G7 countries, have also called for Lai’s release.

He has spent more than five years in prolonged solitary confinement amid, at times, incredibly hot summer conditions. This time does not count toward his two-decade sentence. He reportedly has a litany of health problems that require close monitoring, including diabetes, high blood pressure, heart issues and crippling fatigue. All the while, Lai has been denied independent specialist medical treatment.

While Hong Kong authorities claim his prosecution was a matter of national security, it is clear Lai is merely being punished for participating in journalism and peaceful political activity that criticized the Chinese government.

PASTOR FREED FROM CHINESE PRISON AFTER TRUMP RAISED HIS CASE WITH XI JINPING

If President Xi wants to make a strong impression — and clearly communicate that he is serious about seeking a better relationship with President Trump and the U.S. — he should bring Lai with him to Washington and release him to the care of his family.

Releasing Lai would not automatically settle disagreements over tariffs, Taiwan’s independence, rare earth minerals, technology trade, industrial policy, human rights or a host of other complex issues, but it would be a strong signal of good faith.
